name: CFU/g Calculator
seoDesc: Food, soil and tissue microbiology counts per gram, not per millilitre, and getting from a plate count to CFU/g needs the dilution and the wet weight. Free cf
summary:
Food, soil and tissue microbiology counts per gram, not per millilitre, and getting from a plate count to CFU/g needs the dilution and the wet weight. It returns CFU per gram, log₁₀(CFU/g) and CFU per kg, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator does it, and converts to log CFU/g, the scale used in food safety limits. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the CFU/g
sections.html:
CFU/g = colonies ÷ volume plated × dilution factor ÷ sample weight

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
coloniescolonies on the countable plateCFU
volumevolume platedmL
dilutiontotal dilution×
weightmass of sample in the first dilutiong

sections.title: How do I use the CFU/g?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: colonies counted of 126 CFU, volume plated of 0.1 mL, dilution factor of 10,000 ×, sample weight of 1 g.

Substituting them into the formula gives cfu per gram of 12,600,000 CFU/g, log₁₀(cfu/g) of 7.1, cfu per kg of 12,600,000,000 CFU/kg.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
below 4 log CFU/gLowbelow most spoilage thresholds
4 – 6 logModeratetypical of raw foods
above 6 logHighspoilage or a process failure

  • Log CFU/g is the industry language: 6 log CFU/g is a million per gram.

  • If the sample was frozen or dried, report whether the weight was taken before or after.

  • Homogenisation must be included in the first dilution volume, not after it.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Dividing by the weight twice.
  • Treating a 25 g sample in 225 mL as a dilution factor of 225 instead of 10.
  • Reporting CFU/mL from a solid sample without stating the weight used.

faq.q: How do I convert CFU/g to log CFU/g?
faq.a: Take the base-10 logarithm: 1 × 10⁶ CFU/g is 6 log CFU/g.
Use CFU per swab or per cm² instead; a swab has no meaningful gram weight.

faq.q: What does the CFU/g actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns CFU per gram, log₁₀(CFU/g) and CFU per kg. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
